big_case.notes: Significant Solicitor General emergency application resulting in a 6-page published per curiam opinion (26A560) staying a district court injunction against over 300 miles of border-barrier construction in the Big Bend Sector and clarifying that major-questions-doctrine challenges are statutory rather than constitutional claims under Dalton v. Specter and IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A).

leakage.notes: Forward prediction run on 2026-10-29T21:28:53Z, eleven days before the 2026-11-09 disposition. Retrieval log shows only GovInfo lookups of 8 U.S.C. § 1103 note and CourtListener MCP lookups of Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462 (1994). No outcome material existed or was retrieved.

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, p. 6) grants the application for stay and stays the October 2, 2026 order of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas pending the timely filing and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari.
central_claims.claim: The Court will grant the application for a stay of the October 2, 2026 preliminary injunction pending the filing and disposition of a timely petition for a writ of certiorari.

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, p. 5) grants only a stay pending certiorari rather than summary reversal, expressly noting that the district court did not reach Respondents' alternative nondelegation, Presentment Clause, Take Care Clause, and Due Process Clause claims and that the Court need not reach them now.
central_claims.claim: The Court will decline the government's alternative request to construe the application as a petition for a writ of certiorari before judgment and summarily reverse because Respondents' alternative constitutional claims remain unresolved below.

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, pp. 2-4) holds that § 102(c)(2)(A) strips jurisdiction over non-constitutional claims and relies on Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472-474 (1994), and West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 723-724 (2022), to reject the district court's view that a major-questions claim is a constitutional claim.
central_claims.claim: The government is likely to succeed on the ground that IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A) limits district court jurisdiction to claims alleging a violation of the Constitution, and under Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462 (1994), a major-questions challenge is a statutory interpretation claim rather than a constitutional claim.

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, pp. 4-6) holds that even assuming jurisdiction, § 102(a) and § 102(c)(1) clearly authorize the waivers, rejects reading 'comparatively' into 'areas of high illegal entry' (citing In re Border Infrastructure, 915 F.3d at 1224, and Lomax v. Ortiz-Marquez), and holds that the equities favor the government under Trump v. Sierra Club, 588 U.S. 930 (2019), and TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153, 194 (1978).
central_claims.claim: Even if the merits of the major-questions challenge are reached, IIRIRA § 102(a) and § 102(c)(1) expressly authorize the Secretary to waive all legal requirements for border barrier construction without imposing a comparative-apprehensions test across border sectors, and the balance of equities favors the government under Trump v. Sierra Club.

central_claims.basis: The Court issued a 6-page per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt) that expressly ruled for the government on both the § 102(c)(2)(A) jurisdictional bar and the statutory merits, and no Justice noted a dissent.
central_claims.claim: The Court will likely dispose of the application through a brief unsigned order or short per curiam statement without definitively choosing between the jurisdictional bar and the statutory merits, with two or three Justices potentially noting dissents.
